elements.text: Summary: This paper presents the structural influence of the Si–H functionality on the physicochemical properties of polysilanes. New low-temperature restructuring processes were discovered using thermal analysis (TGA, DSC). Photoluminescent (FL) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements revealed the optoelectronic propertieschemical structure relationship of the synthesized polymers.
Highly reactive Si–H groups lead to restructuring of the main polysilane chain.
Low-Temperature Restructuring Processes in Polyhydrosilanes
Liviu Sacarescu,\*<sup>1</sup> Angeliki Siokou,<sup>2</sup> Rodinel Ardeleanu,<sup>1</sup> Gabriela Sacarescu,<sup>1</sup> Mihaela Simionescu<sup>1</sup>
<sup>1</sup> Institute of Macromolecular Chemistry ‘‘Petru Poni’’, Aleea Grigore Ghica Voda 41A, Iasi 700487, Romania Fax: (þ40) 232 211299; E-mail: livius@icmpp.ro

<sup>2</sup> Foundation of Research and Technology Hellas, Institute of Chemical Engineering and High Temperature Chemical Processes (FORTH/ICE-HT), Stadiou Str. Platani Achaias, P.O. Box 1414, Rion, GR-26504 Patras, Greece
Received: March 16, 2006; Accepted: April 13, 2006; DOI: 10.1002/marc.200600192
Keywords: ESCA/XPS; fluorescence; polysilanes; structure-property relations; thermal properties
Introduction

During the last few decades, due to their ease of processing, many researchers have focused their efforts on the Si-based organic and polymeric semiconductors.<sup>[1]</sup> A part of these is represented by polysilanes which combine the crystalline and organic material properties under the same chemical structure.<sup>[2]</sup> In addition to their p-conjugated carbon homologues, polysilanes show new optoelectronic properties.<sup>[3]</sup> These originate from the s-conjugative character of the polysilane chain combined with the electronic influence ofthe various organic substituents.

Excepting polymethylphenylsilane, polydimethylsilane, and polydiphenylsilane homopolymers are insoluble structures.<sup>[4]</sup> The random scission of their polymeric chains during high-temperature deposition processes leads frequently to materials with structural irregularities and altered optoelectronic properties.<sup>[5]</sup> Therefore, soluble polysilanes with new restructuring properties should open new possibilities to prepare highly ordered optoelectronic thin films on any kind of support. To obtain such materials, continuous efforts have been made in order to discover and investigate new aspects of the structure-electronic properties relationship.<sup>[6]</sup>

This work reports new low-temperature restructuring processes in polysilanes obtained by copolymerization of methylphenyldichlorosilane or diphenyldichlorosilane with methyl(H)dichlorosilane. Information concerning the optoelectronic properties of these materials was further investigated by UV and photoluminescent (FL) measurements.
Experimental Part
Reagents

Diphenyldichlorosilane, methylphenyldichlorosilane, and methyl(H)dichlorosilane (98.5 wt.-%, from Aldrich) were distilled before use. 15-Crown-5 (15C5), (1,4,7,10,13- pentaoxacyclopentadecane) (from Fluka) was dried as described in ref.<sup>[7]</sup>
Measurements

The <sup>1</sup>H and $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$spectra were recorded using a Varian VXR-300 multinuclear spectrometer in CDCl at room temperature. GPC experiments were carried out in THF solution at $3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$at a flow rate of $1 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } \cdot \mathrm { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$using a Spectra Physics 8800 gel permeation chromatograph. FTIR spectra were recorded with an FTS 40A Bio-Rad spectrometer at room temperature in THF solution or in KBr. UV/VIS spectra were recorded in THF solution using a Beckman Acta M4 spectrometer. TGA and DSC analyses were performed using a MOM Paulik-Paulik-Erdey derivatograph and a Mettler DSC12E calorimeter, respectively, at a heating rate of $1 0 ^ { \circ } \cdot \operatorname* { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$, in air.
Excitation and emission spectra were recorded in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { C l }$solution using a Perkin-Elmer Hitachi MPF 43B spectroflu orometer at room temperature.

The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were carried out in an ultra high vacuum (UHV) system, which has been described in detail elsewhere.<sup>[8]</sup> The unmonochromatized AlKa line at 1 486.6 eV and constant analyzer pass energy o ${ \mathrm { 9 7 ~ e V } } ,$giving a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 1.7 eV for the $\mathrm { A u } 4 \mathrm { f } _ { 7 / 2 }$peak, were used in all XPS measurements. The XPS core level spectra were analyzed with a fitting routine that decomposes each spectrum into individual mixed Gaussian-Lorentzian (G-L) peaks after a Shirley background subtraction. The error in the XPS core level peak positions for a good signal to noise ratio was 0.05 eV. The binding energy (BE) scale was calibrated by assigning the main C1s peak at 284.6 eV.
The polymers in the form of powder were pressed in pellets under ambient atmosphere, before their introduction to the UHV system.

The XPS analysis was performed on PSMF and PSHDF. For this purpose polysilane samples were fractioned with a 1/1 mixture of boiling diethyl ether/hexane and considered as sample PSHDF #1 and sample PSMF #2. The low-molecular weight part of PSHDF was recorded as sample #3. XPS spectra showing the core level Si2p photoelectron lines of the samples are presented in Figure 2.

Photoluminescence experiments were performed on PSHDF samples in CHCl solution and compared with results obtained for the PSMF homopolymer. Excitation wavelength was fixed at 367.5 nm for PSHDF and 355.0 nm for PSMF (Figure 3).
Results and Discussion

Polymethylphenylsilane, poly[methyl(H)-co-methylphenyl]- silane, and poly[methyl(H)-co-diphenyl]silane were synthesized through an homogeneous coupling reaction using 15C5 crown ether complex with Na. By this technique, high-molecular weight polymers were obtained in opposition to earlier assumptions which present the sodium metallic particle as a necessary solid support.<sup>[10]</sup>

elements.caption: Scheme 1. Restructuring process of the methylhydrosilyl-segment within the main polyhydrosilane chain.

elements.text: TGA analysis of PSMF homopolymer shows a single decomposition peak at $3 8 8 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$and two thermal decomposition stages for PSHMF and PSHDF with maxima depending more on the Si–H content than on the nature of the substituents (Table 1). This observation leads to the idea that during decomposition, oxidation processes start within the methylhydrosilyl segments leading to a specific restructuration of the polymeric chain.

Further investigation by DSC shows a strong variation of the $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$values proportional to the amount of methylhydrosilyl segments (Table 1, Figure 1). Since higher molecular ratios gave lower $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$values, it was assumed that the methylhydrosilyl fragments represent the flexible part of the polysilane backbone. Unexpectedly, the thermograms of PSHMF and PSHDF show an exothermic peak within $1 0 0 { - } 1 3 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$depending also on the methylhydrosilyl content (Table 1, Figure 1). The specific position in the proximity of the $T _ { \mathrm { g } } ,$the modification of the $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$value in the subsequent DSC runs and the shape of the peak indicate that this transition corresponds to the thermo-induced restructuring of the methylhydrosilyl segments. These processes occur without fragmentation of the main polymeric chain leading to formation of intermolecular bonds (Scheme 1).
To confirm and observe the effects of the restructuring process over the composition and chemical states of solid polyhydrosilanes, further investigations were carried out by XPS analysis.

The survey spectra of PSMF and PSHDF (samples #1, 2, and 3) reveal the Si2p, Si2s, C1s, and O1s photoelectron lines. An estimate of the Si2p BE (Figure 2) in the bonding environment of $\mathrm { ( - S i ( C _ { 6 } H _ { 5 } ) ( C H _ { 3 } ) - ) } _ { n }$can be obtained from the group shift scheme proposed by Gray et al.<sup>[11]</sup> The experimentally observed BE ¼ 100.1 eV (76% ofthe total Si2p signal for sample #2) is very close to the scheme estimate of 100 eV for a Si atom co-ordinated by two other silicon atoms, a phenyl and a methyl group.

elements.text: Concerning the second Si2p peak, according to the same scheme, if one of the two silicon atoms is replaced by oxygen then the Si2p peak would shift for another 0.95 eV resulting in a BE  101 eV, a value that is close to the one experimentally observed.
The C/Si and O/Si surface atomic ratios were calculated from the total intensities of the C1s, Si2p, and O1s peaks, corrected by their atomic sensitivity factors 0.25, 0.27, and

0.66, respectively, and by the inelastic mean free paths of the photoelectrons in question assuming a model semi-infinite solid with homogeneous composition.<sup>[12]</sup> It was found that for sample #2 C/Si ¼ 7.1 which is close to the nominal value for PSMF. The O/Si atomic ratio was 0.43. If for the calculation of the oxygen content only the Si2p peak at $\mathrm { B E = 1 0 1 . 4 ~ e V }$is considered, then $\mathrm { O } / \mathrm { S i } ( \mathrm { o x } ) = 2$suggests that about 24% of the silicon atoms are co-ordinated with two oxygen atoms. In this case, the C/Si ratio close to the nominal indicates that the surface of the sample is slightly contaminated with graphitelike species.

The C1s spectrum of sample #3 consists of two main components at BE ¼ 284.6 eV (C–C, C C, and C–H species) and 286.1 eV (C–O). The weak signal at the high BE side of the main peak (292 eV), is the shake up satellite due to the phenyl groups.<sup>[13]</sup> The Si2p spectrum (Figure 2) shows a high BE component at 104.4 eV (5%) which originates from completely oxidized Si atoms and a component at 101.8 eV representing partially oxidized Si atoms (27%). The O/Si surface atomic ratio is calculated to be 0.82. If only the Si2p peaks with BE ¼ 101.8 and 104.4 eV, are considered then the calculated O/Si(ox) ¼ 3.5 shows that part of the oxygen detected here is bonded directly to C atoms. The C1s peak at 286.1 eV confirms this conclusion. The atomic ratio $\mathrm { C } / \mathrm { S i } = 1 0 . 9 $has been calculated by taking into account the total C1s and Si2p signals is close to 10.6, a value which is expected for a Ph<sub>2</sub>Si/MeHSi ¼ 7/1 molar ratio. The difference is probably due to surface contamination of the sample by residual graphite-like carbon species.

Figure 2 also shows the Si2p spectrum of sample #1. It has been analyzed into four components at BEs 99, 100, 102, and 103.6 eV. The main difference from the Si2p spectrum of sample #3 is the appearance of the peak at 99 eV which represents elemental Si. The intensity of this peak is about 32.5% of the total Si2p signal. The C1s spectrum of the same sample consists of only one component at 284.6 eV (C–C). The C/Si surface atomic ratio for sample #1 is 11.2.

Figure 2 shows the valence band region ofsamples #1, 2, and 3 analyzed with mixed G-L components each one having FWHM ¼ 4 eV. Comparison of the three spectra reveals that at samples #1 and 3 an additional peak appears at BE ¼ 6 eV and can be attributed to Si–Si bonds.<sup>[14]</sup> This peak is very prominent in the case of sample #1, in agreement with the Si2p spectrum that indicates the existence of elemental Si. The peak at 19.5 eV assigned to –C–C– bonds from phenyl groups<sup>[14]</sup> is more prominent at samples #1 and 3. The peak at 4.6 eV (sample #2) has been shifted towards lower BEs (closer to the Fermi level) in the case of sample #1 and 3 (BE ¼ 3 eV).

The presence of oxygen is inevitable since the sample has not been prepared in situ and has been exposed to the atmosphere. Therefore, the oxidized Si atoms resulted from the oxidation reactions with the molecular oxygen trapped inside the solid polymer matrix. These processes take place differently. The increased O/Si(ox) atomic ratios obtained in the PSHMF and PSHDF case resulted from the contribution of the methylhydrosilyl segments which participate in oxidative restructuring even at low temperatures. Moreover, in the absence of molecular oxygen, this leads to the formation of important amounts of elemental silicon as it could be seen for the sample with high molecular weight (sample #1). This enrichment in silicon was observed previously only when polysilanes had been exposed to intensive irradiation with high-energy UV light due to photodecomposition of the –Si– CH bond and the formation of various species of reactive silyl.<sup>[15]</sup>

elements.text: The UV spectrum ofPSMF homopolymer shows an absorption band at 280 nm indicating the presence of s-p transitions due to the phenyl substituent and another at 340 nm corresponding to the $\sigma { - } \sigma ^ { * }$transitions of the conjugated silicon chain which could also be observed in the UV spectrum of PSHMF. Because the position of the absorption maximum in polysilanes depends on the number ofconjugated silicon atoms, it was assumed that the dimensions of the methylphenylsilyl segments in both structures were similar.<sup>[16]</sup> When two aryl groups are attached to the polysilane chain, like in PSHDF, the interaction between the p-orbitals of the phenyls and the s-conjugated silicon chain lead to a decreased optical band gap, causing the absorption maximum to shift to around 350 nm.

Polymethylphenylsilane and PSHDF structures were investigated further by FL measurements. The mirror-image relationship and the bandwidth between absorption and emission give information concerning the regularity of the main chain spatial conformation.<sup>[17]</sup> The FL spectral profile of PSMF with

elements.caption: Figure 3. FL Spectra ofPSMF: (a) PSHDF; (b) in CHCl at room temperature.

elements.text: FWHM ¼ 25 nm is very different from the mirror image of the absorption band at 340 nm indicating that the stiff helical chain conformation of PSMF has frequent irregularities generated by the chiral inversions or twisting from P to M motifs (Figure 3).<sup>[17]</sup> In contrast, PSHDF shows relatively narrow UV absorptions with FWHM ¼ 15 nm and the FL spectral profile closer to the mirror image of the 350 nm absorption band. This is somehow surprising because the small methyl(H)silyl fragments which create bending and fractures of the main silicon chain, should produce a UV absorption maximum shift to lower wavelengths, widening of the bands and strong irregularities in the FL spectra. The absence of such effects indicates that the long diphenylsilyl segments with a stiff and regular helical global conformation<sup>[18]</sup> are coupled through small trans-planar fragments which eliminate the internal conformational tensions allowing a free rotation of the chain around the –Si–Si–Si–Si– dihedral angle of the methyl(H)silyl fragments. Therefore, the s-electron delocalization within the polydiphenylsilane blocks is unaffected by the low temperature restructuring of the small methylhydrosilyl fragments.

In conclusion, insertion of Si–H groups within the main polymer chain opens the possibility to obtain polysilane films with predetermined electronic and mechanical properties. In addition, the high reactivity of the methylhydrosilyl segments leads to unexpected low temperature restructuring that, depending on the gaseous composition of the reaction environment, could be used further to control the intimate composition of the polymer’s surface at atomic level without affecting the optoelectronic properties.
